From GBLUP to Reaction Norms: A Genomic Model Comparison on CIMMYT Wheat

A detailed walk-through with breedRBayes

breedRBayes

03 September 2026

1 Overview

This report walks, in full detail, through a genomic model comparison on the classic CIMMYT wheat dataset that ships with breedRBayes — from a plain genomic BLUP (GBLUP) to a fourth-degree random-regression (RR) reaction-norm model. For every model we show the mathematics, the exact breedRBayes code, the parameter estimates, and an interpretation, and we compare the models on fit (DIC), heritability, genotype ranking and genotype-by-environment (GxE) behaviour.

The engine underneath is Bayesian — every quantity below (variance components, heritabilities, reaction-norm coefficients, reliabilities, selection probabilities) is a full posterior distribution obtained by Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), summarised by its posterior mean and a 95% credible interval.

Table 1. The CIMMYT wheat experiment and the MCMC settings used throughout.
Quantity Value
Genotypes (wheat lines) 599
Environments 4
Records (line x env) 2396
Molecular markers 1279
MCMC iterations / burn-in / thin 5000 / 2000 / 2
Chains 2

The data. 599 CIMMYT wheat lines were evaluated in four environments; a 1279-marker matrix (wheat_M) links the genotypes genomically. The yields are standardised within each environment, so the environment means are flat — but the environments differ strongly in how they rank genotypes (crossover GxE). This is exactly the situation reaction-norm models are built for.

2 The Bayesian mixed-model framework

Every model in this report is a special case of the general mixed model

\[ \mathbf{y} \;=\; \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol\beta \;+\; \sum_{r} \mathbf{Z}_r \mathbf{u}_r \;+\; \boldsymbol\varepsilon, \qquad \boldsymbol\varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\, \sigma^2_\varepsilon \mathbf I), \]

where \(\mathbf y\) is the vector of yields, \(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\) the fixed effects, and each \(\mathbf u_r\) is a random effect with its own covariance structure \(\mathbf u_r \sim \mathcal N(\mathbf 0, \sigma^2_r \mathbf K_r)\).

2.1 Priors and estimation

breedRBayes passes the model to the BGLR Gibbs sampler. The default priors are the standard conditionally-conjugate choices, which give closed-form full conditionals:

\[ \beta_j \propto \text{const (flat)},\qquad \mathbf u_r \mid \sigma^2_r \sim \mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\sigma^2_r\mathbf K_r),\qquad \sigma^2_r \sim \chi^{-2}(df_r, S_r),\qquad \sigma^2_\varepsilon \sim \chi^{-2}(df_\varepsilon, S_\varepsilon), \]

with \(\chi^{-2}\) the scaled inverse chi-square. The Gibbs sampler cycles through the full conditionals, each of which is available in closed form, e.g. for a variance component

\[ \sigma^2_r \mid \cdot \;\sim\; \chi^{-2}\!\Big(df_r + n_r,\;\; S_r + \mathbf u_r^\top \mathbf K_r^{-1}\mathbf u_r\Big), \]

and for the effects a Gaussian whose mean is the usual BLUP-type shrinkage solution. After discarding the burn-in and thinning, the retained draws \(\{\theta^{(1)},\dots,\theta^{(T)}\}\) are the posterior — we report \(\bar\theta = \tfrac1T\sum_t \theta^{(t)}\) and the 2.5/97.5% quantiles.

2.2 Genomic relationships

mrk(gen, wheat_M) turns the raw marker matrix \(\mathbf M\) (coded \(0/1\)) into a VanRaden genomic relationship matrix

\[ \mathbf G \;=\; \frac{(\mathbf M - 2\mathbf p\mathbf 1^\top)(\mathbf M - 2\mathbf p\mathbf 1^\top)^\top}{2\sum_k p_k(1-p_k)}, \]

where \(p_k\) is the allele frequency of marker \(k\). The genomic values are then \(\mathbf u = \mathbf Z\mathbf g\) with \(\mathbf g\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\sigma^2_g\mathbf G)\) — equivalently a ridge regression on markers (RR-BLUP). This is how genotypes that were never observed together still borrow strength through their shared genome.

3 The model ladder

We compare five nested genomic models. All share the same fixed population reaction norm leg(x) and a random environment effect; they differ only in the order of the genotype-specific reaction norm — i.e. how flexibly each line is allowed to respond to the environmental gradient \(x\).

Table 2. The five genomic models, from plain GBLUP (M0) to a quartic reaction norm (M4).
Model Name Genotype term Meaning
M0 GBLUP (order 0) \(g_i\) (intercept only) Plain GBLUP: one genomic value per line, no GxE slope
M1 RR linear (1) \(g_i + b_{i1}L_1(x)\) Linear reaction norm (genomic Finlay-Wilkinson)
M2 RR quadratic (2) \(g_i + b_{i1}L_1(x) + b_{i2}L_2(x)\) Quadratic reaction norm (curvature allowed)
M3 RR cubic (3) \(+\,b_{i3}L_3(x)\) Cubic reaction norm
M4 RR quartic (4) \(+\,b_{i4}L_4(x)\) Quartic reaction norm (saturates 4 environments)

3.1 Model M0 — plain genomic BLUP

\[ y_{ij} \;=\; \mu + f(x_j) + g_i + E_j + \varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad \mathbf g \sim \mathcal N(\mathbf 0, \sigma^2_g\mathbf G),\; E_j \sim \mathcal N(0,\sigma^2_E). \]

Each line has a single genomic value \(g_i\) (its overall genetic merit); the fixed term \(f(x_j)=\mu+\beta_1 L_1(x_j)+\dots\) is the population response to the environment. There is no genotype-specific slope — GBLUP assumes every line reacts to the environment in the same way.

3.2 Models M1–M4 — genomic reaction norms

We let each line’s genetic value change smoothly along the environmental gradient \(x\) (here the leading GxE axis, see below):

\[ y_{ij} \;=\; \mu + f(x_j) + \underbrace{g_i + \sum_{k=1}^{q} b_{ik}\,L_k(x_j)}_{\text{genotype reaction norm } v_i(x_j)} + E_j + \varepsilon_{ij}, \]

where \(L_k\) are orthonormal Legendre polynomials on \([-1,1]\) (so \(L_1\) is linear, \(L_2\) quadratic, …), and \(q\) is the model order (1–4). The line-specific coefficients are genomic:

\[ \mathbf g \sim \mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\sigma^2_g\mathbf G),\qquad \mathbf b_k \sim \mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\sigma^2_{b_k}\mathbf G), \]

i.e. each Legendre coefficient is itself a GBLUP effect, so slopes are predicted even for lines with few records by borrowing across the genomic relationship matrix. The genotype’s reaction norm is the curve \(v_i(x)=g_i+\sum_k b_{ik}L_k(x)\); its intercept measures broad adaptability and its slope measures responsiveness to the environment.

3.3 The environmental gradient

Table 3. The environmental index x (leading GxE axis).
env x
1 E1 -1.486
4 E4 0.304
2 E2 0.575
3 E3 0.607

Because yields are standardised within environment, the Finlay–Wilkinson index (the environment mean) is flat. We instead use the leading GxE axis — the first environment score from a singular-value decomposition of the genotype × environment matrix — as \(x\). Environment E1 sits far from the others (it ranks lines very differently), so \(x\) has genuine spread and the reaction norm has something real to model.

4 Fitting the models

The entire ladder is five bbglr() calls. mrk(gen, wheat_M) is the genomic main effect (the intercept), and mrk(gen, wheat_M):leg(x, q) its reaction-norm interaction:

library(breedRBayes)
data(wheat); data(wheat_M)
rel  <- list(wheat_M = wheat_M)
ctrl <- bbglr_control(nIter = 5000, burnIn = 2000, thin = 2, nChains = 2)

# Environmental index x = leading GxE axis (first env SVD score), added to `dat`.
# (see report source for the SVD; classic FW would use the environment mean.)

# M0  plain GBLUP -------------------------------------------------------------
M0 <- bbglr(yield ~ leg(x), random = ~ mrk(gen, wheat_M) + env,
            residual = ~ units, data = dat, relmat = rel, control = ctrl)

# M1..M4  add a genomic reaction norm of order q ------------------------------
M2 <- bbglr(yield ~ leg(x),
            random = ~ mrk(gen, wheat_M) + mrk(gen, wheat_M):leg(x, 2) + env,
            residual = ~ units, data = dat, relmat = rel, control = ctrl)
# ... M1 uses leg(x, 1), M3 leg(x, 3), M4 leg(x, 4)

Every downstream number in this report comes from the extractor functions:

varcomp(M2)                                        # variance components (+ K matrix)
heritability(M2, genetic = "mrk(gen, wheat_M)")            # h2 of the intercept
heritability(M2, genetic = "mrk(gen, wheat_M):leg(x, 2)")  # per-coefficient h2
model_fit(M2)                                      # DIC, pD, R2, RMSE, reliability
solution(M2, term = "mrk(gen, wheat_M)")           # genomic values (GEBVs)
reaction_norm(M2, term = "mrk(gen, wheat_M):leg(x, 2)")    # per-line curves
rr_gradient(M2, term = "mrk(gen, wheat_M):leg(x, 2)")      # across-gradient analytics
gxe(M2,  term = "mrk(gen, wheat_M):leg(x, 2)")             # adaptability/responsiveness/stability

5 Model comparison: which order fits best?

The Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) trades goodness of fit against model complexity, \(\text{DIC} = \overline{D(\theta)} + p_D\), where \(\overline{D}\) is the posterior-mean deviance and the effective number of parameters \(p_D = \overline{D(\theta)} - D(\bar\theta)\) measures how much the extra coefficients actually cost. Lower DIC is better. We also report the residual variance \(\sigma^2_\varepsilon\), the in-sample \(R^2\) and RMSE.

Table 4. Model-fit ladder. Lower DIC is better; the star marks the winner.
Model Description DIC pD R2 RMSE varE
M0 GBLUP (order 0) 6491.35 150.40 0.24 0.88 0.83
M1 RR linear (1) 5893.21 375.26 0.53 0.70 0.59
M2 RR quadratic (2) 5813.53 454.70 0.59 0.67 0.55 ★
M3 RR cubic (3) 5823.76 486.80 0.60 0.66 0.54
M4 RR quartic (4) 5830.62 509.49 0.61 0.65 0.54

Figure 1. DIC across the model ladder. The dashed line marks the minimum; going beyond it buys complexity (pD) without a better fit — the classic over-parameterisation signature, expected here because there are only four environments.

Reading Figure 1. The DIC drops as soon as we allow a genotype-specific slope, then flattens. Because the trial has only four environments, a reaction norm can have at most a handful of identifiable shape parameters — the cubic and quartic terms add pD (complexity) without improving fit. The winning model is RR quadratic (2) (M2); we use it (or the quadratic M2) for the biological interpretation below.

6 Variance components

varcomp() returns the posterior of every variance component. For the reaction-norm models it additionally returns the realised across-genotype coefficient covariance matrix \(\mathbf K\) — the (co)variances of the intercept and each Legendre slope — which is what actually drives GxE.

The environmental variance captures the (small, because standardised) spread of environment means; the residual \(\sigma^2_\varepsilon\) is the within-line noise; and the genomic components (intercept + slopes, plus their covariances in \(\mathbf K\)) are the heritable signal. A negative intercept–slope covariance would mean high-yielding lines tend to be less responsive (a stability/productivity trade-off).

7 Heritability of the reaction norm

Broad-sense genomic heritability is the fraction of phenotypic variance explained by the genomic effect. For a single coefficient \(c\) (the intercept, or a Legendre slope) breedRBayes computes, in every MCMC draw,

\[ h^2_c \;=\; \frac{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(c)}{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(c) + \sigma^2_\varepsilon}, \]

using the corresponding diagonal element of \(\mathbf K\), and summarises the resulting posterior. heritability(fit, genetic = "mrk(gen, wheat_M):leg(x, q)") returns one heritability per coefficient.

Interpretation. The intercept heritability (Table 6) is the reliability of overall merit and is stable across models. The slope heritabilities (Table 7) tell you whether the responsiveness to the environment is itself heritable — i.e. whether you can select for GxE. Higher-order coefficients typically have low, poorly-estimated heritability here, another sign that four environments cannot support a quartic curve.

8 Reaction norms: how genotypes respond to the environment

The heart of the model. Each line’s predicted genetic value is a curve across the environmental gradient, \(v_i(x) = g_i + \sum_k b_{ik} L_k(x)\). Where curves are parallel there is no GxE; where they cross, the ranking of genotypes changes between environments — the essence of crossover GxE.

Figure 2. Genomic reaction norms for a random sample of 120 wheat lines (quadratic model M2). The thick red dashed line is the population mean response. Fanning and crossing of the thin lines is genotype-by-environment interaction; vertical ticks mark the four real environments.

9 Ranking genotypes and how the ranking changes

9.1 Does the order of the model change who wins?

Figure 3. Spearman rank correlation of the genomic intercepts (overall merit) between models. Near-1 values mean the models agree on overall ranking even though they disagree about GxE.

9.2 Per-environment ranking (crossover GxE)

Overall merit is not the whole story: because the reaction norms cross, the best lines change from environment to environment. Below we take the top lines by overall merit and track their predicted rank in each real environment (from the M2 curves evaluated at each environment’s \(x\)).

Figure 4. Bump chart: predicted rank (1 = best) of the top-15 overall lines in each environment, ordered along the gradient. Lines that stay flat are broadly adapted; lines that swing are responsive/specialists.

10 GxE descriptors: adaptability, responsiveness, stability

gxe() condenses each reaction norm into three breeder-facing numbers:

  • Broad adaptability — the average genetic value across the gradient (the intercept-like level; higher = better everywhere).
  • Responsiveness — the linear slope \(\mathrm{cov}(v_i,x)/\mathrm{var}(x)\) (how strongly the line tracks the environment).
  • Stability — the coefficient of variation of the curve, \(\text{CV}_{ge}=100\,\mathrm{sd}(v_i)/|\overline{v_i}|\); lower CV = more stable across environments.

11 Selection probabilities for the best model

A point GEBV tells you where a line ranks; it does not tell you how sure we are. Because the fit is Bayesian, we can answer the breeder’s real question directly: what is the probability that a line is truly among the best?

pr() computes this from the posterior. In every MCMC draw it re-ranks all 599 lines and flags the top fraction; the selection probability is the fraction of draws in which the line makes the cut:

\[ P_i(\text{top } \alpha) \;=\; \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \mathbb{1}\!\left\{\, u_i^{(t)} \;\ge\; Q_{1-\alpha}\big(\mathbf u^{(t)}\big) \right\}, \]

where \(u_i^{(t)}\) is the genomic value of line \(i\) in draw \(t\) and \(Q_{1-\alpha}\) is the \((1-\alpha)\) quantile of that draw’s values. The ranking is redone within each draw, so the probability is unaffected by centering and honestly propagates posterior uncertainty. The call is a one-liner:

pr(M2, term = "mrk(gen, wheat_M)", type = "random", threshold = 0.10)  # P(top 10%)
pr(M2, term = "mrk(gen, wheat_M)", type = "random", pair = TRUE)       # P(A beats B)

Figure 6. Selection probability vs point GEBV for all 599 lines. Colour is P(top 20%). Lines high on the y-axis are confident selections; a high GEBV sitting low on the y-axis is a high-risk pick whose ranking the data cannot yet pin down.

Why this matters. Ranking on GEBV alone treats a knife-edge difference the same as a decisive one. The probability separates lines the data are sure about from lines that merely happened to land on top of a noisy point estimate — the difference between a safe advance and a gamble.

11.2 Head-to-head comparisons

pr(..., pair = TRUE) gives the full matrix of pairwise win probabilities \(P(A \succ B) = \tfrac1T\sum_t \mathbb 1\{u_A^{(t)} > u_B^{(t)}\}\). Below, for the top-12 lines by merit, is the probability that the row line beats the column line:

Figure 7. Pairwise win probability P(row beats column) among the top-12 lines. Deep values near 1 (or 0) are decisive; cells near 0.5 (pale) are statistical ties — the two lines are genetically indistinguishable on these data.

Reading Figure 7. Rows are ordered best-to-worst by GEBV. Where the top block is uniformly dark the leader genuinely dominates; where cells fade toward 0.5 the “ranking” between two lines is a coin-flip and either could be advanced without regret.

12 Conclusions

  • Genomics works. Linking the 599 lines through the 1279-marker genomic relationship matrix lets every line borrow strength across the genome; the genomic intercept heritability is the reliability of overall merit.
  • A reaction norm beats plain GBLUP on this data: allowing a genotype-specific slope lowers the DIC, and the winning model is RR quadratic (2) (M2).
  • But more is not better. With only four environments, cubic/quartic terms add complexity (pD) without improving DIC and give poorly-estimated, low-heritability slopes — the ladder makes the over-parameterisation visible.
  • GxE is real and it re-ranks. The reaction norms cross (Figure 2), the best lines change between environments (Figure 4), and gxe() separates broadly-adapted all-rounders from responsive specialists (Figure 5).
  • Rank with probabilities, not just point estimates. pr() turns the posterior into the probability that a line is truly a top selection (Figure 6) and into head-to-head win probabilities (Figure 7), so a confident advance can be told apart from a coin-flip between statistical ties.
  • Everything is a posterior. Each estimate above carries a credible interval from the MCMC draws — heritabilities, variance components, reaction-norm coefficients, selection probabilities and rankings all come with honest Bayesian uncertainty.

Generated with breedRBayes on the bundled CIMMYT wheat / wheat_M data. Reproduce with report/run_wheat_comparison.R then knit report/wheat_model_comparison.Rmd.
